passage:
A weekend camp asked students to give up phones for two days. Many felt nervous at first.
Without phones, they played cards, hiked, cooked together, and talked before sleeping. Some missed music and messages. Others felt relieved.
On the last day, students discussed what they had learned. Most did not want to abandon phones completely, but they wanted more control.
One student said, "My phone is useful, but I do not want it to be my only way to rest."
The camp was not against technology. It was a mirror. It helped students see habits that had become automatic.
